description_full: Mako Mining Corp. engages in mineral exploration and exploitation activities in Nicaragua, the United States, and Guyana. The company explores for gold and silver deposits. Its primary asset is its 100%-owned San Albino mine comprising the San Albino and the Las Conchitas gold deposits, which consist of five mineral concessions covering an area of approximately 22,422 hectares located within the San Albino-Murra Property in Nueva Segovia, Nicaragua. The company was formerly known as Golden Reign Resources Ltd. and changed its name to Mako Mining Corp. in November 2018. Mako Mining Corp. was incorporated in 2004 and is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.

financial_summary: Mako Mining Corp is a small-cap basic materials business with a $648M market cap on $148M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +33% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +15.1pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 39% against a 10% cost of capital — a 29-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 43%.

The business throws off $41M in free cash flow — roughly 27 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.57× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 54× is fortress-like.

Net dilution runs at 5.9% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 2.7% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 27pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.81x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 65% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 22% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 33% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 54% and a beta of 1.01, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 2.56 vs 5y 1.02), so read it loosely.
About $1.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 34% in the 2020 crash and 75% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 42% below its DCF fair value of $12.74, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 6%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $6.18 to $27.09 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Basic Materials peers: P/E 12.5 vs 16.3, EV/EBITDA 6.2 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 15.9 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.3% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 11.0% annual cash-flow growth, 14pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 39% clears the cost of capital of 9.6% by 29pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.19).
It runs a 43% gross margin and converts 27% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.57x.
ROE of 22% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 25% last year, worth watching.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $77.4M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 8.6, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 32.8% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.7%, and institutions hold 53%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-5.9%), diluting holders.
